mainIssue: The plan's own success metrics are unfinished: slide 28 ships literal x placeholders for target volumes and the 20-30% income promise on slides 3 and 28 has no baseline, method or source.
criticalFixes: Replace the x placeholders on slide 28 with one computed target volume per livelihood.
Anchor the 20-30% income target to a stated baseline of current household income and name the source.
Remove the beekeeping paragraph from the bio-charcoal slide and run one full proofing pass.

findings.title: The success metrics the whole plan answers to are placeholders and unsourced targets
findings.principle: Evidence Grounding: every headline number needs a source
findings.diagnosis: Slide 3 promises an income increase and slide 28 sets the accountability frame for 36 months of work, but the volume targets still contain the letter x where numbers should be and the income figure carries no baseline, no method and no source.

evidence.quote: volume (e.g. x kg of salt, x
average household can see about 20 -30% income increase

findings.why: The milestone slide is the contract between Riverside and the client. A funder who reads x kg of salt concludes the targets were never computed, and every other number in the deck inherits that doubt.
findings.reflect: Take one livelihood, say salt. What data would you need to set a real 36 month volume target, and where would the income baseline come from to defend the 20 to 30% claim?
findings.fix: Compute one real target per livelihood from the pilot scale already chosen on slide 16, state the current household income baseline next to the percentage and name a source for both. Where a number cannot be grounded yet, label it an assumption to validate in phase 1 instead of shipping an x.

findings.title: A beekeeping paragraph ships twice on slide 19 and again on the bio-charcoal slide
findings.principle: ERIP Performance: the deck is the product
findings.diagnosis: The same beekeeping training paragraph appears twice on slide 19 and then reappears word for word on slide 25, whose title is about scaling bio-charcoal production. The body of a cost slide opens with bee colony lifecycle content.

evidence.quote: Scaling bio-charcoal production can be costly
Beekeeping training includes understanding the entire bee colony lifecycle, hive management,

findings.why: A client who spots one pasted leftover stops trusting the slides they cannot verify. A single visible QA miss taxes every claim in the deck, and this one sits on a cost slide where trust matters most.
findings.reflect: What end of project check would have caught this before the client did, and who on the team owns that pass?
findings.fix: Strip the duplicated paragraph, then run one full proofing pass where a teammate who did not build the slides reads every body block against its title.

findings.title: Unit costs are quoted but never become a budget or a decision
findings.principle: ERIP Performance: does it change outcomes?
findings.diagnosis: Slide 19 prices beekeeping per person and slide 25 prices bio-charcoal per ton with a range spanning more than four times, yet no slide multiplies these into a program budget, names a funding source or sets the ceiling at which a livelihood is too expensive to pilot.
findings.why: Riverside cannot allocate capital from a unit cost range. Without a total and a funding plan the cost research stays trivia and the go or no go decision lands back on the client.
findings.reflect: At the pilot scale you would recommend for bio-charcoal, what do the low and high ends of that per ton range mean in total dollars, and at which number would you advise against the pilot?
findings.fix: Add one cost roll-up per livelihood: pilot scale times unit cost, the funding source it maps to and the ceiling above which Riverside should defer that livelihood. Ranges are fine, a missing total is not.
